3. That he, apart from this which is granted to him, refrain from any and every other involvement with the said Sisters; in the governance and direction of whom no mission may be admitted that is not recognised and consented to by the diocesan ordinary.

Florence, 31 August 1877

C. Luigi Ciaranfi

3. Letter of priest Pietro Campolini to the Archbishop of Florence Mons. Eugenio Cecconi, 16 November 1877, Florence, ACF - Daughters of St. Anne (Proc. p. 627).

In this letter, Fr. Campolini criticises the Prior Attilio Giovannini, who became protector of the Daughters of St. Anne out of "cunning."

I.M.I.

Monsignor,

On the happy occasion of your name-day, I feel it my duty to wish Your Most Reverend Excellency many prosperous years of life, full of every blessing and happiness, temporal and spiritual, for your own good and for the good of this Diocese; Deus exaudiat.

I take this fitting occasion to inform you in writing (since it is so hard to have an unhurried face-to-face conversation with Your Excellency) that I too have learned from others what Prior Giovannini was writing to you about the Daughters of St. Anne, and that his withdrawing to become their protector is a stroke of cunning, since he saw he could not come out of it cleanly otherwise.

As for myself, I say and repeat what I said before; and I ask Your Excellency to do as my predecessors did.

And, kissing your Holy Ring, I ask your pastoral blessing and declare myself

of Your Most Reverend Excellency,

Florence, Via del Fosso No. 22, 4th Floor

16 November 1877

Your most humble and devoted son in JC.

Pietro Campolini

4. Five letters from Canon Luigi Ciaranfi to the Archbishop of Florence Mons. Eugenio Cecconi, Florence, ACF - Monasteries, copy in AFSA C.3.165.

a) 18 February 1878 (Proc. p. 628).

In this first letter, Canon Ciaranfi reports that the priest Lazzeri insists on wanting to resign the office of confessor to the Daughters of St. Anne.

He met with the Prior of S. Lorenzo, Attilio Giovannini, who complained about these Sisters and especially about the local superior, Sister Anna del Salvatore Orsi, calling her "false and a liar." He asks that the Sisters be required either to submit to the Bishop's authority or to leave.

Most Reverend Excellency, Mons. Archbishop

Mons. Vicar wishes me to write to Your Excellency on behalf of the Sisters of St. Anne, because Fr. Lazzeri insists on resigning, and says he cannot in conscience continue to exercise his ministry with them. Yesterday I saw Mons. Giovannini, Prior of S. Lorenzo, and he began speaking to me of the said Sisters, who are in his parish, showing himself little satisfied with them and, in particular, with the local superior, false and a liar. He told me that he did not see clearly into their way of conducting themselves, and feared some remark that might compromise the priest attending to them. He asks that a remedy be found, by requiring either that they submit to the direction given them by the diocesan Ordinary, or that they leave. Having told Mons. Vicar that Your Excellency would indeed take this matter up with the Superior General, who is actually in Rome, he would like to know something about it, in order to act accordingly.

As for the Dorotheans, unfortunately that superior was attempting a coup, but the Lord did not allow it; and there was time to warn Mons. Vicar, who stopped everything, cautioning Mr. Antonino Ciardi not to lend himself to anything without a special order from Your Excellency. Mr. Secretary Fei, on his return to Florence, can inform you even better about it, should Your Excellency think it well.

Meanwhile I implore the Pastoral Blessing, and with deep respect I have the honour to remain.

Of Your Most Reverend Excellency,

From the Archiepiscopal Curia of Florence

18 February 1878

Your most humble and obedient servant and subject

C. Luigi Ciaranfi

b) 28 February 1878 (Proc. p. 629).

Canon Ciaranfi reports that the Foundress of the Daughters of St. Anne wrote to him warmly recommending her Sisters to him. The local superior, Sister Anna del Salvatore Orsi, came to visit him. He gave her a few general cautions and promised a visit; the superior thanked him in an "exalted and comical" manner.

He considers it wise to hear all the Sisters of the community.

The parts of the letter not relevant to our case are omitted.

Most Reverend Excellency, Mons. Archbishop

[omissis]

Sister Gattorno wrote to me warmly recommending her Sisters to me; I replied at once that I had received an order from Your Excellency to see to them in a special way, and that I would do my best, trusting in their docility and cooperation.

The superior here came to see me; and I tried, kindly, to give her some general cautions, and then promised that I would go visit the Institute. At this news she leaped with joy, and in a comical, exalted manner, showered me with thanks and praise. And we shall see! Fr. Lazzeri no longer intends to leave; on the contrary, he wishes to stay, because he hopes for a good effect from the superiors' action. I am thinking of holding a hearing, which Mons. Vicar also approves; following which it will be possible to see what needs to be done. [...]

I humbly implore the Pastoral Blessing, and with deep respect I have the honour to remain

Of Your Most Reverend Excellency,

Florence, 28 February 1878

Your most humble and obedient servant and subject

C. Luigi Ciaranfi

c) 24 March 1878 (Proc. p. 631).

In this letter, Canon Ciaranfi informs the Archbishop that the Vicar General has ordered Fr. Ottavio Andreotti not to go to the house of the Daughters of St. Anne any longer; Provincial Zini was satisfied with this prohibition; Fr. Andreotti, for his part, insisted on the need to help the Sisters with the school.

The elderly priest Baldassarre Fini has agreed to go celebrate Mass for the Sisters, replacing Fr. Andreotti.

From this letter too, the parts not concerning our Servant of God are omitted.

Most Reverend Excellency Mons. Archbishop

[omissis]

Mons. Vicar ordered Fr. Andreotti not to go to the House of the Sisters of St. Anne any longer; the said Father received the order with apparent ease, but not without insisting a little on the need to render some service to the Sisters for the Schools. Monsignor stood firm on the prohibition, which also satisfied Fr. Zini. By Monsignor's order, I spoke with old Fr. Fini, and he undertook to go say Mass every day, except on feast days, following the arrangement practiced by Fr. Andreotti. I believe Fr. Lazzeri is in Rome; at least he told me he intended to come, but I have not seen him since. [...]

I implore the Pastoral Blessing, and with deep respect I have the honour to remain

Of Your Most Reverend Excellency,

Florence, 24 March 1878

Your most humble and obedient servant and subject

C. Luigi Ciaranfi

d) 13 April 1878 (Proc. p. 633).

Canon Ciaranfi has learned from Fr. Giovanni di S. Firenze that two Sisters, Daughters of St. Anne, behaved with little modesty while attending a sick woman, so he will go to their house to admonish them all. He saw a rather vain young woman leaning out of their window and learned that she will go to the novitiate. He hopes that the appointment of a new Cardinal Protector will improve the Sisters' life, that their rules will prove satisfactory, and that the confessors may be able to have some influence over the good order of the house.

The Sisters have absolute trust in the Foundress. Fr. Andreotti no longer visits them.

The parts not concerning the Sisters Daughters of St. Anne are omitted.

Most Reverend Excellency, Mons. Archbishop

[omissis]

As soon as possible, I shall go to the Sisters of St. Anne, to deliver, with due delicacy, a little reproof, having learned from Fr. Giovanni di S. Firenze that, when two Sisters went to sit up through the night with a sick penitent of his, they did not restrain themselves with the reserve, or rather modesty, required not only of religious persons but of Christians in general. Recently, passing through Via Faenza, I saw a postulant leaning out of the House's window, and she seemed to me a rather vain young woman; I saw the Superior for a moment, and she told me this young woman was only passing through, on her way to the Novitiate in Piacenza. Following Cardinal Berardi's death, perhaps these Sisters will have some other Most Eminent Protector; let us hope their arrangement improves, that the rules prove satisfactory, and that the Confessors may have some influence over the good order and morality of the House. If Your Excellency could, or thought it fitting to do something for these Sisters in this regard, I believe some benefit might come of it. They hold the superior general in high regard and blindly do whatever she suggests. Fr. Andreotti has withdrawn entirely. [...]

Meanwhile I kiss your sacred Ring, and with deep respect I have the honour to remain.

Of Your Most Reverend Excellency,

Florence, 13 April 1878

Your most humble and obedient servant and subject

C. Luigi Ciaranfi

e) 27 April 1878 (Proc. p. 635).

The Foundress of the Daughters of St. Anne has been in Florence to carry out the change of Superior.

The new superior, Sister A. Santina Solinghi, often goes to confer with Fr. Andreotti.

This Institute, Canon Ciaranfi says, gives cause for concern, and there is no way to keep watch over it, since its rules prevent the confessor from concerning himself with its external affairs, whether regarding the Sisters or the house.

He also gave the Sisters a reproof concerning modesty in caring for the sick.

The Vicar General charges him to ask that he request Cardinal Franchi, their protector, to remove these Sisters from Florence.

The parts of the letter not concerning the Servant of God are omitted.

Most Reverend Excellency, Mons. Archbishop

[omissis]

Sister Gattorno came to Florence, and Fr. Andreotti went to meet her at the station; but he did not go to the Sisters' House. The said superior changed the Florence superior. She gave the Sisters a talk, telling them that only she, and no one else, is to be informed of any difficulties that may arise within the Institute, which is purely lay and therefore has no dependence whatsoever on ecclesiastical Authority. She flatly denied to Fr. Fini that she had committed herself to Mons. Archbishop to pay an alms to the priest who would go there to celebrate; and she told him to have the alms given to him by whoever had invited him to go there to say Mass. Fr. Fini no longer wished to go; but Mons. Vicar asked him to continue, granted him about thirty Masses from the Pious Legacies, but does not intend to continue this grant, being displeased with this woman's conduct, which obliges me to inform Your Excellency, with the request that you take action.

This Superior and Foundress has a son who idles about Florence and often goes to the Institute. She also has a married daughter; and, when the latter comes to Florence, she settles in at the Institute with her husband and a little daughter of hers, staying there for a few days. The new superior of Florence often goes, almost every day, to S. Giovannino, to confer with Fr. Andreotti, who thus continues, even from a distance, to run the Institute. The physician Baccani, an honest man who serves other Monasteries, has resigned from serving these Sisters because of the unworthy way they treat the sick Sisters.

Fr. Giachetti of S. Firenze told me that two Sisters, while sitting up through the night with a sick woman, his penitent, took certain liberties with her, cum tactu in pectore, and she had to call them to order; they also began taking liberties with each other, in the very presence of the sick woman, who no longer wanted them near her. Passing through Foligno recently, I saw a young woman leaning out of a window of the Institute, dressed in a rather showy manner.

Of these two incidents I informed the Superior, from whom I learned that the young woman was a postulant who had been sent back home, certainly for lacking a vocation; as for the incident reported by Fr. Giachetti, she told me she believed those Sisters were no longer in Florence, since the Mother General has changed many of the personnel; she promised she would take the proper steps so that it would not happen again; but I went to the Institute the Monday after Easter, called all the Sisters together, and urged upon them the good example, the reserve, and the modesty that must always accompany them in performing the acts of charity they render to the sick.

It is certain that this Institute gives food for thought and for concern; nor is there any way to watch over it, since the only way there would be, namely that of the Confessor, is closed off, their Rules wanting him kept entirely apart from the whole external conduct of the individuals and of the Institute. This is clear both from the fact itself and from that printed instruction they are accustomed to hand over to the Confessor, which Your Excellency knows.

The Superior told me that, after Cardinal Berardi's death, they came to have the Most Reverend Franchi as their protector. Mons. Vicar wishes Your Excellency to speak with him about these Sisters, asking him, if possible, to remove them from here; for Monsignor fears that sooner or later some disorder might arise that would cause us embarrassment and serious trouble. In any case, Mons. Vicar would like to wash his hands of this matter, and no longer concern himself with it. [...]

Meanwhile I humbly kiss your sacred Hand, and with deep respect I have the honour to remain

Of Your Most Reverend Excellency,

Florence, 27 April 1878

Your most humble and obedient servant and subject

C. Luigi Ciaranfi

5. Letter of the Archbishop of Florence Mons. Eugenio Cecconi to the Foundress Rosa Gattorno, 4 May 1878, Rome, Capranica College, AFSA F.7.59 (Proc. p. 638).

On the basis of information received from Florence, the Archbishop urges the Mother Foundress to dissolve the Florence house as soon as possible and without publicity.

Rome, from the Capranica College, 4 May 1878

Reverend Mother,

I am most sorry to have to tell you, also following recent news that has reached me from Florence, that the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne, as presently constituted, cannot in my diocese produce the good that it seemed at first it would. Although I sincerely wish that it establish itself in a way that truly answers to the holy purpose it has in view, I find myself, nonetheless, after mature reflection, obliged to ask you, Reverend Mother, as I hereby do ask you, to take the necessary steps so that, little by little and without publicity, but as soon as possible, the Florence House be dissolved. In this way the matter will pass unnoticed, as your own interest requires.

Awaiting an acknowledgment of receipt of this letter, I remain with due regard

Of You, Reverend Mother,

Most devoted

† Eugenio Archbishop of Florence

6. Letter of the Foundress Rosa Gattorno to the Archbishop of Florence Monsignor Eugenio Cecconi, undated but probably from 5-6 May 1878, AFSA Foundations, Florence (Proc. p. 641).

The Mother Foundress, having received the order to gradually withdraw the Sisters from the Florence house, expresses deep sorrow and astonishment, unable to understand the causes, especially since the Vicar General had told her that nothing serious was involved. She also sets out the good that is being done there and defends the Sisters in a heartfelt way, asking forgiveness.

She is ready to go to Florence, subject to the Archbishop's own authorisation.

Your Excellency,

I have just finished reading your most precious letter and reply by return post. My God! The wound it caused me is such that I do not know how I shall manage to put together these few lines, for which I first of all ask forgiveness for the effort it will take you to understand what I am about to say to you.

Your Most Reverend Excellency, however much I think about the reason for such terrible news, I cannot manage to understand it; if it were the matter concerning the Sister who left430, this, if it had been reported to Your Most Reverend Excellency accurately, could surely not be the reason.

For I, passing through Florence, thought it best to change the Superior [Sister del Salvatore], and so I did, but I heard a voice, indeed more than one, saying: "Remove the Superior, and the house will blow up too. Ah! We shall see to it that this happens"; I did not wish to worry about this, I went to her Vicar, as well as to the Canon, and found none of this to be true.

The Vicar assured me that there was nothing to it, that I had done well to change the Superior, and that what had happened (his very words) was a childish prank.

As for the Sister's case: finding herself placed under strict discipline by the new Superior, she began to complain; and what did she do? She went out alone, going to the Confessor... she was certainly being backed.

He took her to Ciaranfi, and the superior, once informed, went and fetched her, and took her away, at once catching the train for Piacenza. If this is so wicked a deed as to deserve infamy, I do not believe it!!!

And Your Most Reverend Excellency is too wise not to take into account what spiteful and slanderous people are capable of doing, as for example, while I was in Florence, two incidents involving the Sisters of Charity were being reported, concerning two girls, who even had to appear before the Magistrate, and nothing was done to them; I arrived here, and another Sister of Charity had run off with a young man, and nothing happened; and I report these things about the said Sisters.

Your Most Reverend Excellency, ah! Have pity on this your most poor servant, who has always been so devoted to you, and who, in everything, was sincere and obedient towards you. Why punish me so harshly? Without first issuing a command?

Listen, Your Most Reverend Excellency, I shall go at once to Florence, and shall stay there a good while, and shall keep Your Most Reverend Excellency informed of everything, and you will advise me on whatever displeases you, and I shall try to remove it.

A house that did and still does so much good: the schools were inspected by the Superintendent, who was pleased, so much so that the Municipality granted it a stipend, and the boarding pupils are truly numerous, as are the sick. I have the most beautiful letters of thanks, I do not have them here, but I read them in Florence; so many are the requests that I had to send two more Sisters; Providence is most generous.

Your Excellency, ah! For pity's sake, put a priest in charge of giving the Holy Exercises, so that you may be informed of the truth about the good spirit there. I cannot bear to think of so sad a thing, it tears my soul apart; and if in the past you were pleased with the house, you will be so again. Believe me, much good is being done.

Not long ago, they managed to have a poor wretch, after many years of a wicked life in which he would hear nothing of priests or God, die in the arms of Holy Religion. And how well instructed the girls are in the Catechism! If you saw them, you would be pleased.

Ah, no! I do not want to think of this sad news. It grieves me too much! I trust in your fatherly clemency, which you have always shown me; meanwhile I am informing the Protector whom the Holy Father, in his goodness, gave to the Institute, this being approved by Holy Church; I must report everything and await what is commanded, just as, before leaving here, I await a few lines from you to set my mind at ease and tell me that I shall always be a small part of your flock.

Meanwhile, wretched as I am, I shall not cease to pray to the good God to grant you all those graces that Your Most Reverend Excellency desires.

Your Excellency, you well know that the Institute has 52 houses, and I can assure you in all truth that I have never had the slightest complaint from the diocesans, and in every Diocese they are not content with one house, nor with two; I am forced to refuse requests. Make inquiries about the Houses of Naples, Pistoia, etc.

Your Excellency, a line, for pity's sake, for I can think of nothing else!! Ah! Your charity grants me everything, it seems to me I already have what I desire: your forgiveness along with your Holy Pastoral Blessing, while, prostrate at your feet, full of veneration, I remain of Your Most Reverend Excellency

Your most humble and devoted Servant

Sister A. Rosa Gattorno

P.S. As soon as I have your letter, I shall leave at once.

7. Two letters of the Foundress Rosa Gattorno to Cardinal Alessandro Franchi, protector of the Institute, Florence, ASV Secretariat of State, year 1878, Rubric 284; copy in AFSA C.3.165.

a) 19 May 1878 (Proc. p. 638).

In this letter, the Mother Foundress sets out the suffering caused in Florence by the slanders reported to the Curia. She states that the confessor wants to turn the community into an enclosed convent and, in confession, speaks ill of the Institute's Superiors. The same confessor, moreover, took into his own house a Sister who was ill and weak of mind, who wanted to go home, and accompanied her to the Vicariate.

The Vicar for nuns unfortunately believes all the accusations leveled against the House.

Your Most Reverend Eminence,

I hope you have read my letter, which I sent you through a Sister, together with the Institute's prospectus.

I write now in great distress over a tribulation that has arisen here in Florence, where I had to go yesterday because of certain slanders, and indeed quite insipid falsehoods, reported to the Curia, which I can assure you have no basis in truth whatsoever.

But first of all, allow me to tell you frankly that the confessor is the cause of the whole trouble; for he would like to turn it into an enclosed convent, and, finding himself thwarted, he stirs up trouble of every kind; and finally, there being a Sister whose convulsions left her a little weak in the head, and who decided she wanted to go home, he took her into his own House, and then accompanied her to the Vicariate, telling the Superior that she was there, and the Superior went to fetch her, accompanying her to Piacenza; from this incident he has emboldened himself, saying that there is not enough supervision, adding a thousand absurdities, which I can assure you were all invented by him, and that, in confession, he does nothing but speak ill of the Superiors to the Sisters, trying to make them lose their vocation. The worst of it is that the Vicar for nuns believes him.

Your Most Reverend Eminence well knows that we are in no way bound to submit to internal direction from the confessor. He must do nothing but hear confessions, and nothing else; for now I add nothing more. Should matters worsen further, I am resolved to come to your feet and tell you in person, in all truth, how things stand, and Your Most Reverend Eminence will surely defend your own work and save your most poor Daughter, while she asks for the Pastoral Blessing and, prostrate, remains of Your Most Reverend Eminence

Florence, 19 May 1878

Your most humble and obedient Daughter

Sister A. Rosa Gattorno

b) 23 May 1878 (Proc. p. 639).

Mother Gattorno, having been in Florence for a week, was able to observe that everything was proceeding regularly: the pupils at the school are numerous, the boarding school is growing, and requests for care of the sick are so many that not all can be met. Despite this, new slanders keep arising and being reported to the Archbishop, who is in Rome, and she begs the Cardinal Protector to assure Mons. Cecconi that such accusations are false.

Your Most Reverend Eminence,

How grieved I am, and what cruel torment my soul suffers, I cannot express. Under the oppression of slanders that are freshly contrived every day, and then written to the Archbishop who is there.

Ah, for pity's sake, Your Most Reverend Eminence, say a word to Mons. Archbishop, and assure him that what has been reported to him is not true; as for what I have heard of the slander, I can likewise assure you, in all truth, that in these six days that I have been in this house, having made the most minute observations on the good conduct of both the rule and the schedule, everything proceeds in the most exact order; the schools are overflowing, the boarding school keeps growing, and the sick are so numerous that requests have to be turned down every day.

If Your Most Reverend Eminence thinks I should come to Rome, write to me, and I shall obey at once; I would already have done so, but what prevented me was my frail health, which these days, by God's mercy, suffers more than usual.

Your Most Reverend Eminence! Send me a word from you to set me at ease, for I need it most urgently; blessed God will repay you a hundredfold with His graces for the charity you show to this poor Servant of yours.

Prostrate at your feet, she implores your pastoral blessing, while, full of veneration, remains of Your Most Reverend Excellency

Florence, 23 May 1878

Your most obedient Daughter

Sister A. Rosa Gattorno

8. Letter of Father Mauro Ricci of the Pious Schools to the Archbishop of Florence Mons. Eugenio Cecconi, 29 May 1878; ACF - Monasteries (Proc. p. 640).

Fr. Ricci asks the Archbishop not to believe everything he is told regarding the Daughters of St. Anne of Florence, since there are no serious faults, only trifles.

He points out that Canon Ciaranfi cares above all about his own authority.

My dearest friend,

Ciaranfi cares about the authority you have delegated to him; I care about yours, and about your name, which I should like to see honoured as it deserves.

I do not think it a suitable means to this end, the way certain fussy and touchy people behave, who, out of womanish gossip and trifling nothings, construct an argument to tell a Religious Institute: destroy yourself with your own hands. In short, that is all the demands concerning the Sisters of St. Anne amount to.

Do not believe, I beg you, everything that worthy men contrive, who, for lack of experience, are capable of knowing neither the world nor the monastery. The test of an extraordinary Confessor suits your kindly nature, not that of an autocrat. Try it, or better still, change the Confessor altogether. I tell you this because it grieves me to see the weight of other people's rashness fall upon you, innocent as you are.

Come back soon; appear unexpectedly at some ceremony in the Cathedral, meanwhile letting the announcement of the Visit circulate. And if it seems to you that I am being impudent, give me a penance, and note it down in your notebook, writing: "To Mauro Ricci, such-and-such a penalty, because he will not restrain his excessive affection for me..."

Turning now to some amusing news, I must tell you that I have finally had to accept the rectorship of the Pellegrino; but my residence is still always in Florence, where I await you soon so as to confirm myself once more

Yours

Mauro Ricci

29 May [1878]

9. Letter of the Foundress Rosa Gattorno to Card. Alessandro Franchi, 30 May 1878, Florence, ASV Secretariat of State, Year 1878, Rubric 284 fasc. 2 (extra-procedural).

Because of the aforesaid slanders, the Archbishop has ordered the withdrawal of the Sisters from Florence. Mother Gattorno begs him to defend her daughters and invites him to the Mother House.

Your Most Reverend Eminence,

I cannot express to you the sorrow I feel at seeing that, over such insipid slanders, Archbishop Cecconi has pronounced an unwelcome sentence, that of leaving his Diocese and retiring. My God! Over such trifling things, and, to say it all, mere pettiness of a...!!!

Moreover, our Parish priest, a most distinguished person, Mons. Giovannini, parish priest of S. Lorenzo, is ready to give any certificate, both regarding the care of the sick and the schools, and he has sometimes also been confessor.

Your Eminence! Because of one person who wrote to the Archbishop whatever he saw fit, must the poor Institute be made to suffer such a blow?

Your power, joined to that great wisdom in acting well, will surely take up the defence of your Daughters.

Your Most Reverend Eminence! For pity's sake, give me just one line from you to take this burden from me. I would have to return to the Mother House. May I go in peace? I no longer say I shall come to Rome, because I cannot bear the heat and would do nothing but take to my bed; I am suffering greatly.

Oh, if only I could have you in Piacenza, and be able to tell you so very many things, Your Eminence! May I hope for it? Grant me this charity. My God! Am I being too bold? Just one word, with your pastoral blessing, while, prostrate at your feet, I remain of Your Most Reverend Eminence

Your obedient Daughter

Sister A. Rosa Gattorno

Piacenza, 30 May 1878

10. Letter of the Foundress Rosa Gattorno to the Archbishop of Florence Mons. Eugenio Cecconi, [7 June 1878, Piacenza], ACF-Monasteries, copy in AFSA C.3.165 (Proc. p. 643).

She asks forgiveness: she is ready to take the punishment upon herself and do penance; but she begs that the Florence house be spared.

Your Most Reverend Excellency,

Although I understand it to be almost an insolence to dare send you my writings, I also well know that, you being the Pastor of a distinguished Diocese, which you occupy so wisely, I cannot help thinking that, prostrating myself at your feet and imploring you, I shall still find in you the Father and benefactor I had for a good three years.

Correct me, punish me if it was I who caused that poor house to be struck down by so great a punishment. Ah! For pity's sake, forgive the house and punish me; tell me what I have done, and I am ready to do the penance.

I would have flown to your feet in Rome; but I reached Florence, and then the fever would not leave me, and I had to turn back, although I am still very ill; it would surely be a good thing for the work that... God do with me as He wills.

Mons. Giovannini promised me that he too would say a word. Your Most Reverend Excellency, believe that what touches the house are slanders; as for me, ah! I am an abyss of infamy!!! Unworthy even to be called a Christian. Woe is me! Poor Servant of the Lord!

A word of forgiveness for the house, and for me the punishment, while I prostrate myself at your feet, asking for your Pastoral Blessing, with bowed head I remain, with veneration, of Your Most Reverend Excellency

Your most humble and devoted Servant, Sister A. Rosa Gattorno

I enclose a copy from Fini.

11. Letter of Mons. Attilio Giovannini, parish priest of San Lorenzo in Florence, to the Foundress Rosa Gattorno, 8 June 1878, Florence, ASV, copy in AFSA C.3.165 (Proc. p. 644).

The parish priest is very distressed at the Sisters' situation in Florence and points out to Gattorno that she herself was unable to learn even a single charge worth discussing, since everything is wrapped in a veil of mystery that suggests the gravest matters, which in fact do not exist.

For his part, he could issue a certificate in the Sisters' defence, but it would carry no weight. He therefore suggests that the Cardinal Protector manage to have the matter referred to the Holy See; meanwhile he is ready to testify to the favour the Sisters enjoy among the people.

Most esteemed Mother,

I am deeply grieved at the turn the matter has taken today, all the more since, from news received here from a reliable source, it appears to me that the case has already been decided in advance. You came to Florence to find out what the grounds of accusation against the poor Sisters were, and you were unable to obtain a clear and precise statement of even one that was worth discussing; not even your requests to have impartial persons who could examine the facts exactly and report on them were accepted; the very respectable people who came forward to ask for fairer assessments were turned away; the whole thing, in a word, revolves in a mystery of accusations which cannot, and never will be able to, be disproved, precisely because they are wrapped in a mysterious veil that makes their seriousness seem immense.

In this state of affairs, I do not understand what use a certificate could be, which I could only make in a negative way. It would be more decisive if the Most Eminent Protector managed to have the cause referred to the Holy See and to appoint an apostolic visitor. I do not at all hesitate to testify to the good opinion the Sisters enjoy and have always enjoyed among the people, as well as to their having always responded, in every circumstance, with charitable service according to the spirit of their Institute, without there ever having been any complaint whatsoever. All this I can always say truthfully; but to this one can always reply: I received the accusations, and you do not know how matters stand. I repeat to you that, if the Most Eminent Cardinal Protector refers them, without further examination, to the Ordinary's discretion, I see the affair's success as very unlikely.

Be patient and have the fullest confidence in God's mercy, which will not allow a new scandal in our city and such grave harm to the Institute. I have the honour to remain

Your most devoted

A. Giovannini

Florence, 8 June 1878

12. Letter of the Foundress Rosa Gattorno to Card. Alessandro Franchi, undated but probably from 10-11 June, Piacenza, AFSA C.3.165, original in ASV Secretariat of State, Year 1878, Rubric 284 fasc. 2 (extra-procedural).

The Foundress sends Card. Franchi a certificate from Mons. Giovannini as testimony to the slanders against the Sisters of the Florence house, and renews her invitation to him to come to Piacenza.

Your Most Reverend Eminence,

I have just now received the letter from Mons. Giovannini, parish priest of S. Lorenzo in Florence, from whom I had requested a certificate. He replies to me in the terms that Your Most Reverend Eminence will see from his letter, which I enclose for you, keeping a copy. Believe me, Your Eminence, that they are all slanders. I have also been told that now everything has been laid on me. For this I bless God, so long as nothing is suffered by the work of the Lord. There are 52 houses, and never in twelve years has such a thing happened, and all of them, by God's mercy, are doing well.

Your Eminence! Make the sacrifice of coming here, so that you may examine everything well and punish me, if you find things I have not done well. Yesterday Mons. Bishop [of Piacenza] told me there was every likelihood that Your Most Reverend Eminence would come among us. He would like to know the date, and I too join in asking you most earnestly to let us know, so that I could gather all the Superiors together and Your Most Reverend Eminence will hear from them how things stand, and Mons. Bishop will give them the Holy Exercises.

Meanwhile this unworthy servant of the Lord makes and will keep making earnest pleas to be relieved of the burden she drags along so poorly, and I shall cease to be an obstacle to a greater good, always obedient to submit myself to any labour, and glad to be able to give, for the work of my God, my last breath.

A line from you, I hope to obtain everything from your charity, while I prostrate myself at your feet asking for your pastoral blessing, with the utmost veneration I remain of Your Most Reverend Eminence

Your most humble and obedient Servant

Sister A. Rosa Gattorno

13. Letter of Mons. Attilio Giovannini to the Foundress, 18 June 1878, Florence, ASV, copy in AFSA C.3.165 (Proc. p. 645).

Mons. Giovannini explains why the Archbishop of Florence, Mons. Eugenio Cecconi, is so unyielding: he is being negatively influenced by certain persons and listens to no one else. He suggests that both the Bishop of Piacenza and the Cardinal Protector should personally take up the Institute's defence: this would be the best course.

Florence, 18 June 78

Most esteemed Mother,

Do not be overly distressed by the tribulation God has sent you, whose only purpose is to better establish the Institute, and by no means its ruin. For now the matter is proceeding administratively, as was fitting, and I do not despair that everything will be smoothed out in this way. It does not surprise me that the Archbishop remains firm in his judgment; unfortunately this is his habit, which has been the chief cause of his undoing in the diocese. He listens to no one but those three or four suspicious courtier-like individuals who play him to their own advantage, afterwards leaving the whole responsibility on him.

Here no one is respected; it is enough to contradict in order to be cast out and held in suspicion by the malign influence of the few counselors who maneuver in the shadows and ruin everything. The prudent keep silent and only trust that the truth will make its own way, and that Rome will remedy the disorder. Hence certificates would be most effective if requested by Rome, but presented by you they would only compromise the persons who had made them, because the Archbishop would dismiss them as suspicious persons who had come forward because they were interested in the accusations, or because they were deceived and manipulated with no knowledge whatsoever of the case. Moreover, since the accusations concern not so much the Florence house as the whole Institute, it seems to me that the whole defence ought to be mounted by that Mons. Bishop, as Apostolic Delegate, and by the Most Eminent Cardinal Protector; and in this proceeding, should Mons. Bishop wish to have information to send to Rome, and wish it from me or from any other person, he himself ought to write, and for my part I would answer with complete sincerity. Since the matter is going well, let us not spoil it by diverting it from the right course it has taken. Should this road prove entirely exhausted, with no other means of negotiation left, there would still remain another legal recourse, namely a personal appeal to the Sacred Congregation; but I believe it will not be necessary to resort to this extreme measure of defence.

Here things are going very well, and I keep urging the greatest caution and prudence, so that nothing may happen that could give rise to complaints from the confessor or others.

Fr. Zini is convinced, as I am, that this is the best course of action in this matter: recollection, silence, caution and good graces in Florence; energy and firmness in Rome; present your defences against the heads of accusation, suggest the means of learning the true state of affairs, insist on this examination of the facts, cite also the persons who can give information; but then leave all the care of appealing to the Delegate Bishop or to the Most Eminent Protector, who will judge whether it is opportune to resort to this means.

You must understand that a certificate, in this cause, would be an act hostile to the Archbishop, and ought not to be made except at the request of one who has the authority to call for it. Be at peace, as I am at peace: the more one flails about, the more entangled one becomes. Pray for me.

A Jesuit Father who has long been in Piacenza, I know to be very favourably disposed towards the Institute; try to interest him on your behalf. Here Fr. Iacoboni, to whom I related the affair for advice, was most sorrowful and astonished at it.

[Mons. Attilio Giovannini]

14. Letter of the Foundress Rosa Gattorno to Cardinal Alessandro Franchi, probably from June 1878, Piacenza, AFSA C.3.165, original in ASV Secretariat of State, Year 1878, Rubric 284 fasc. 2 (extra-procedural).

Writing to Cardinal Franchi, Mother Gattorno encloses Mons. Giovannini's letter. The Bishop of Piacenza has also written to Archbishop Cecconi.

Your Most Reverend Eminence,

I cannot express to you what sorrow it is to me to have to trouble you continually with these tiresome letters of mine, always over the Florence matter. Having written again to Mons. Giovannini, as well as to the Father Provincial of the Scolopi, in order to obtain some certificate about that house, Mons. Giovannini replies to me, and I enclose his letter for you. May Your Most Reverend Eminence keep it with you.

The Bishop of Piacenza has already written three times to the Archbishop of Florence, and the last time, yesterday, quite forcefully, and he said that today he would also write to Your Most Reverend Eminence, certain heads of accusation having reached me that are truly false, most false, and I find it useless to copy them out for you, because they are of no account.

Be so good as to grant me your pastoral blessing, that it may give me strength to stand firm, as I felt great relief on receiving your most venerable letter, although it contained no word to make me hope I might have you here.

I am truly indiscreet and too bold, but to obtain so great a grace, I know well that it cannot be had except through unceasing entreaties.

While I prostrate myself and, with the utmost veneration, kiss your hand, remaining of Your Most Reverend Eminence

Your most humble and obedient Daughter

Sister A. Rosa Gattorno

15. Letter of the Archbishop of Florence Mons. Eugenio Cecconi to the Foundress Rosa Gattorno, 30 June 1878, Rome, Capranica College, AFSA F. 7.59 (extra-procedural).

With this letter the Archbishop answers the petition presented by the Foundress (cf. supra, p. 177) and confirms that he cannot depart from the provisions communicated to her.

He sets 31 October as the final date for the Sisters' withdrawal.

Reverend Mother,

You will already have heard from Canon Ciaranfi that I cannot depart from the provisions I communicated to you in my letter of 4 May last.

This grieves me greatly, but accept this cross with resignation, and God will reward you by enlightening you ever more on the proper means of rightly directing the Institute you have founded.

Seeing no sign informing me that you have begun to carry out what I wrote to you, and, on the other hand, wishing to give you the means of doing so with all possible decorum, I set as the final term the 31st of October of this year, that is, the day on which, according to Florentine custom, the rents paid in February fall due. Once that term has passed, the Daughters of St. Anne will cease to be recognised as a religious Family in my diocese, and consequently the faculties granted to the assigned Confessor, and the privileges that the Holy See grants at the discretion of the local Ordinaries, will lapse.

I sincerely implore from God every kind of grace for you, and, blessing you with all my heart, I remain

Of You, Reverend Mother

Most devoted

† Eugenio Archbishop of Florence

Rome, 30 June 1878

16. Letter of the Foundress Rosa Gattorno to Archbishop Mons. Eugenio Cecconi, 5 October 1878, Piacenza, AFSA C.3.165, originals in ACF Firenze, Monasteries, Daughters of St. Anne, fasc. 2 (extra-procedural).

The Mother Foundress asks the Archbishop, in derogation of the order to withdraw the Sisters from the Florence house, to grant them a further period of trial.

Piacenza, 5 October 1878

Your Most Reverend Excellency,

In the hope that Your Most Reverend Excellency will be willing to receive favourably a humble prayer of mine, I make bold to insist once more in commending to you the house of the Sisters of St. Anne in Florence.

I have never been able to persuade myself that Your Excellency would carry out the order communicated to me to leave the House of Florence; yet, the deadline assigned to me for carrying out that order now drawing near, I consider it my duty to beg you once more to make yet one further trial of the due submission, mine and my Sisters', to Your Excellency's authority.

Therefore, be so good as to give me whatever instructions you, in your wisdom, judge suitable for the good conduct of that House, and that are in harmony with the spirit of the Institute itself.

Confident of obtaining everything from Your Most Reverend Excellency's immense charity, I prostrate myself at your feet, asking for your pastoral blessing, while, full of veneration, I remain

Your most obedient Servant

Sister A. Rosa Gattorno

17. Letter of Archbishop Mons. Eugenio Cecconi to the Foundress Rosa Gattorno, 22 October 1878, Florence, ACF - Monasteries, copy in AFSA Foundations, Florence (extra-procedural).

Overcoming his initial misunderstanding, the Archbishop grants the humble petition the Foundress has requested, and allows her, with benevolent spirit, the further period of "trial" she had proposed to him.

This will remain, from now on, his attitude towards the Sisters and the Institute (cf. supra, p. 158).

Reverend Mother,

I do not wish to reject the warm and respectful petition you address to me in your most esteemed letter of the 5th of this month, that a further trial be made of the due submission, yours and your Sisters', to ecclesiastical Authority.

Nothing, indeed, is more in keeping with the desires of my heart than to find the Daughters of St. Anne residing here worthy of my fatherly benevolence.

Let them have a filial trust in me, who, though unworthily, bear the character of their Pastor, and everything will proceed as it ought.

The excellent Mons. Giovannini, who enjoys my fullest confidence, will assist you with his wise counsel. Thus I hope the trial will come to a good conclusion.

In this sweet hope, I bless you with all my heart, and I remain

Your most affectionate in the Lord

† Eugenio Archbishop of Florence

Florence, 22 October 1878

18. Letter of the Foundress Rosa Gattorno to Archbishop Mons. Eugenio Cecconi, 24 October 1878, Piacenza, AFSA C.3.165, original in ACF, Monasteries, Daughters of St. Anne, fasc. 2 (extra-procedural).

Mother Gattorno thanks him for the letter and expresses gratitude, obedience, and submission.

She asks the Lord to reward the Archbishop for the good he does the Institute through his protection.

Piacenza, 24 October 1878

Most Reverend Excellency,

You cannot imagine what consolation your most venerable letter has brought me! I do not reply in my own hand, because my unsteady health does not allow me to do so today, nor do I wish to delay in offering you the expression of my most heartfelt and sincere gratitude.

Most Reverend Excellency, in my littleness I find no words sufficient to attest to you all the gratitude of this poor Institute for the immense charity you have kindly granted it: I leave it to the Lord to stand in my place, and I go forward assured that God, considering not our prayers, which surely are worth little or nothing, but the merits of the most venerable prelate for whom we pray, will wish to give you an ample reward for all the good you do this poor Institute by extending to it your protection.

Your Most Reverend Excellency will find in the poor Daughters of St. Anne the most devoted submission. I have written to the Superior of the Florence House to come and prostrate herself at your feet and receive your most venerable orders, and I hope that, with the help of the Lord and of our Holy Mother, Your Most Reverend Excellency will find in us, in future, submissive daughters eager to make themselves worthy and deserving of your protection.

Bless the whole Institute, and her who, prostrate at your feet, full of veneration, remains of Your Most Reverend Excellency

Your most devoted Servant

Sister A. Rosa Gattorno

19. Extract from the "Memoirs" of the Foundress Mother Rosa Gattorno, December 1876, in AFSA A.2.31, pp. 490-491 (extra-procedural).

Mother Gattorno recounts having received a higher light during Mass, which enlightened her as to the cause of the disturbance in the Florence Community.

I went to one of our houses [Florence] and received from the confessor strong complaints about the superior; certain things from inside the house he knew, and one could not understand how, or who had told him.

The Sisters were suspected, but as for certain other [persons], one could not think it was they, because they loved her greatly, she being very good. There were certain small faults, but certainly not as he had said: that he ought to warn the Archbishop... He knew so many things that one could never imagine where they came from. They showed me, that very first evening, a young woman who wanted to become a Sister, but towards whom I felt a strong repugnance. [...]

On the very morning I was to leave, no sooner had I made my communion than my God told me clearly that it was this young woman who concocted such ugly things, and then told them to the confessor, slandering the superior and the girls.

As soon as I came out of church, as soon as I could, I told the superior, and an effort was made to remedy such horrendous monstrosities.

The truth came out: that she had already done the same thing elsewhere, and the poor superior had to be admonished by the Archbishop. Oh goodness of a God, who can ever uncover such hidden intrigues but You, who are uncreated wisdom? You who see into the most remote hiding places of the human heart?

20. Anonymous handwritten letter received by the Foundress Mother Rosa Gattorno, undated, AFSA C.3.163 (extra-procedural).

The writer accuses the Servant of God of immoral conduct that casts discredit on the Community; she therefore suggests that the Mother Foundress remedy this promptly, by removing her from Florence.

Madam,

All over Florence people do nothing but talk about one of your Sisters who has had a child, and everyone says it is the superior. Believe me, these are real scandals. You will hear that within a few days the public papers... Do something to remedy this scandal, you whom they say is such a holy woman.

Get rid of her, this scandalous woman, for the others suffer for it too, since they will become the laughingstock of everyone. And it was being said around Florence that that Sister was too forward. But that she could do such disgraceful things and behave like a prostitute, and discredit all your daughters, that was not expected. Before the public papers speak of it, and the police take an interest, remedy it; heed the advice of one who wishes you well. Otherwise it may happen that they expel all of you. Think seriously about it. One does not trifle with Florence. Put in another, more serious and level-headed woman, to restore order; this one has now made you lose so much credit that everyone speaks ill of the Sisters of St. Anne.

Forgive the liberty I have taken. I always used to give alms to your daughters, but now I no longer do, and not even my husband wants me to go near there while that filthy woman is involved. And many other gentlemen of Florence share this same opinion. What scandals! What goings-on! Now the convents have been reduced to houses of brothel and prostitution, forgive the expression.

But remedy it quickly, it is in your own interest. We hope you will profit from the lesson of one who cares about you.
